prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, changing our understanding of who exports and invests abroad and how trade affects productivity and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus foreign direct investment moved trade theory from representative-industry models to selection among heterogeneous firms. That shift changed how the gains from trade, reallocation and exporter premia are understood. It also fits the micro data that researchers use. Two decades on, the framework has been tested against firm-level evidence, structurally estimated and carried into quantitative policy work. It is a distinct advance from the new trade theory recognised in 2008. A framework that survives repeated empirical confrontation is the kind of result I weigh most heavily. I keep B030 first after reading the round of openings. The strong support for B001 persuades me that trade is a serious field this year, but it has not changed my view of which trade contribution is better established empirically.
statement.case_against: The main weakness is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum established the exporter facts and built closely related models, and none of them is credited on this ballot. Melitz's contribution is centred on one landmark paper, which some colleagues will find narrow. Helpman is also on B001, so supporting B030 competes with the candidacy that currently has the broadest backing. The empirical premium and selection patterns also predate the theory. The contribution is therefore a unifying framework more than a discovery of new facts.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B001 first but notes that empirical support for the protection-for-sale predictions is mixed. He also says the committee may prefer to reward trade through the firm-heterogeneity line instead.
responses.response: I agree that the empirical record matters here. Mixed support for the structural predictions of protection for sale is a reason to prefer the firm-heterogeneity line, which has been tested more densely against micro data. I do not think it is decisive against Grossman and Helpman, because their endogenous-growth and trade work stands apart from that one model. I keep B001 as an alternative for that reason. Still, if the committee must pick a trade contribution, I would put the more extensively confronted framework first.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B030 second and treats Melitz as central and Helpman as the natural co-recipient. He flags the gap left by Bernard, Eaton and Kortum, and says Helpman's presence on two ballots could split support.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The Bernard-Eaton-Kortum gap is real, and I cannot resolve it within the three-name limit without weakening the Melitz-Helpman core, so I leave it as a stated reservation. On the split, I do not think the two trade ballots are competitors in a scientific sense. They credit different contributions by the same person. A committee choosing between them should do so on which contribution is better established and more cleanly attributed. Splitting credit across them would not be a sound reason to prefer either.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B030 seventh. He sees Melitz's contribution as a single central paper that refines rather than overturns older models, and notes that the empirical exporter facts were found earlier and independently.
responses.response: The point about the exporter facts is fair and is why I treat attribution as the main weakness. I would qualify the claim that it only refines older models. Selection of firms into exporting changes the welfare accounting of trade liberalisation. It also changed which data researchers collect and how quantitative trade models are built. The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple paper on exports versus foreign direct investment broadens the base beyond one paper. I accept that this is a narrower contribution than B001 in breadth of reach.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B018 first. She values the combination of new data, credible designs and a conceptual framework, and acknowledges debate over shock-based identification and long-run persistence.
responses.response: I share her appreciation of the empirical designs, and B018 was in my own top eight. I ranked it lower because of the shift-share identification questions she lists. Added to those are uncertainty over how to split credit between the trade-shock and task strands and overlap with the 2024 prize. If the committee wants a labour-and-trade award, I would back a narrow citation to the trade-shock evidence rather than a blended one. For now I judge the firm-heterogeneity framework to rest on firmer ground.

uncertainties: Whether credit for the firm-heterogeneity framework can be defended without Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.
How the committee would treat Helpman's presence on both B001 and B030, and whether a citation could be drawn so that it does not overlap with a Grossman-Helpman award.
Whether Melitz's contribution is broad enough for a prize on its own or needs the wider Helpman programme.

How much weight to give mixed empirical support for the protection-for-sale predictions when comparing B001 with B030. My reading of colleagues' assessments is based on their written statements, and I have not independently checked the empirical literature.
Whether B017 (Chetty and Hendren) is mature enough this year. I rank it second but still see it as recent, with place-effect estimates whose replication by independent users is still developing.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My profile documents no collaboration or institutional tie with the credited persons. I did hold Harvard-based research and fellowship positions from 2006 to 2017, and some credited candidates may have Harvard affiliations. That is a general institutional overlap, not a personal or professional connection, and the profile does not establish one.
